3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was what they had been warned to expect, and fearing that the tempter had talked them out of the faith. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding, and they long to see Paul as he longs to see them.

Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.” He cannot thank God enough, and prays night and day to see them and fill the gaps in their teaching. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will clear his road to them, make their love overflow to everyone, and strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness when Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unable to bear the silence any longer, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his fellow worker, to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be shaken by their troubles. Paul had warned them that suffering was part of the Christian calling, and it had come. He sent Timothy for fear that the tempter had shaken their faith and his work had been wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as Appointment, Not Accident

The key word in verse 3 is keimetha — we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the language of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted, and Paul uses the same root of himself in prison, put there for the defence of the gospel (Phil 1:16). Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God's attention; it is a placement.

That is the pastoral logic, and it needs stating carefully. What steadies a shaken believer is not the promise that the trouble will stop but the assurance that the trouble is not a mistake. If hardship means the plan has gone wrong, every difficult week is evidence against the faith. If hardship is where God has laid you, the difficult week proves only that you are where he put you. The Reformed tradition has held this consistently: God governs all things, his people's afflictions included, and such suffering is purposeful — producing endurance, character and hope (Rom 5:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v.3) — faith is usually lost by erosion, not by renunciation.

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and its absence is a cruelty disguised as encouragement (v.4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 3 shows a pastor’s heart in anxiety and relief. Unable to bear not knowing how the young church was doing under persecution, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was to be expected and fearing that the tempter had shaken them (vv. 1–5). Then Timothy returned with wonderful news of their faith and love and their longing to see Paul. Paul was comforted in his own troubles: now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord (vv. 6–8). He overflows with thanks and prays night and day to see them again and supply what is lacking in their faith (vv. 9–10). The chapter ends with a prayer: that God would open the way for Paul to come, make their love increase, and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his saints (vv. 11–13).

Therefore when we could bear it no longer. Key words. “Bear” (stegō, endure, hold in). Paul’s concern became unbearable.

We were willing to be left behind at Athens alone. Key words. Paul went from Berea to Athens (Acts 17:15–34). “Left behind” (kataleipō, abandoned): a costly sacrifice. In a hostile, idol-filled city, he chose to be alone so that they could be helped.

And we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ. Key words. High praise: God’s fellow worker. Some manuscripts read “God’s servant,” as the ESV notes. Timothy was young but trusted.

To establish and exhort you in your faith. Key words. “Establish” (stērizō, strengthen, make firm, like propping up a building). “Exhort” (parakaleō, encourage). New believers need follow-up care.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul doubted God. He knew new believers under pressure need support.

In a sentence. So when we could stand it no longer, we thought it best to be left by ourselves in Athens. We sent Timothy, who is our brother and co-worker in God’s service in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith,

On a Tuesday. Who is a young or struggling believer you could help strengthen this week? Go, call or write.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.

That no one be moved by these afflictions. Key words. “Moved” (sainō, shaken, or perhaps fawned upon, lured away). Persecution can shake faith, or tempt people to compromise to escape it.

For you yourselves know that we are destined for this. Key words. “Destined” (keimai, appointed, set). Suffering is part of God’s appointment for his people (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12; John 16:33). Not a sign that God has abandoned them, but part of his plan. Knowing this in advance protects from shock.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in his people’s pain. It means he uses it for their good and his glory (Romans 8:28; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

In a sentence. so that no one would be unsettled by these trials. For you know quite well that we are destined for them.

For worship. If you are suffering, it is not a sign God has forgotten you. Trust him in it.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.

For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction. Key words. Paul did not promise an easy life. He warned new converts to expect trouble. Honest evangelism counts the cost (Luke 14:28).

Just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. Key words. The warnings came true.

For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith. Key words. Paul’s personal anxiety (“I”).

For fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you. Key words. The tempter is Satan (Matthew 4:3). He uses suffering to tempt believers to give up.

And our labor would be in vain. Key words. If they fell away, Paul’s work would have been empty.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can be lost. Paul feared that their faith might prove false, which would show his labour fruitless. Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

In a sentence. In fact, when we were with you, we kept telling you that we would be persecuted. And it turned out that way, as you well know. For this reason, when Paul could stand it no longer, he sent to find out about your faith. He was afraid that in some way the tempter had tempted you and that our labours might have been in vain.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, be honest about the cost. And pray for those under pressure to give up.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy has now come back with good news of their faith and love, and their warm memories and longing to see Paul. That news has comforted him in his own distress; it is like new life to him to know they stand firm in the Lord. He cannot thank God enough for the joy they bring him, and he prays earnestly to see them again and supply what their faith still lacks. He prays that God will open the way, that the Lord will make their love for one another and for everyone overflow, and that he will strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness before God at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Persons, One Verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb — the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man's prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v.10) was not sincerity but completeness — the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but ‘for all’ (v.12) — the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.

But now that Timothy has come to us from you. Key words. Timothy rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5).

And has brought us the good news of your faith and love. Key words. “Brought good news” (euangelizomai, the gospel word). The report was itself like a gospel to Paul. Faith and love: their relationship to God and to others.

And reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you. Key words. The slanders had not turned them against Paul.

For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith. Key words. Paul was suffering in Corinth too. Their faith comforted him. Believers comfort one another by standing firm.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s comfort depended only on them. It came from God, through them (2 Corinthians 7:6).

In a sentence. But Timothy has just now come to us from you and has brought good news about your faith and love. He has told us that you always have pleasant memories of us and that you long to see us, just as we also long to see you. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and persecution we were encouraged about you because of your faith.

For worship. Thank God for good news of others’ faith. Your faithfulness might be someone else’s comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.

For now we live. Key words. Paul feels alive again, renewed. Their faithfulness brings him life.

If you are standing fast in the Lord. Key words. “Standing fast” (stēkō, standing firm). In the Lord: their strength is in him. The “if” is also a gentle encouragement to keep standing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s spiritual life depended on them. It expresses how deeply his joy was bound up with them.

In a sentence. For now we really live, since you are standing firm in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Stand firm in the Lord today. Others are encouraged by it.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?

For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you. Key words. Paul cannot thank God enough. Their faith is God’s work.

For all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God. Key words. Joy in God’s presence.

As we pray most earnestly night and day. Key words. “Most earnestly” (hyperekperissou, superabundantly, beyond measure). Intense, persistent prayer.

That we may see you face to face. Key words. Letters are not enough. He longs to be with them.

And supply what is lacking in your faith? Key words. “Supply” (katartizō, complete, mend, equip). Their faith was real but young. They needed more teaching, which chapters 4–5 begin to give: on holiness, love, and Christ’s return.

What it does not mean. It does not mean their faith was defective. It means it was growing and needed more instruction.

In a sentence. How can we thank God enough for you in return for all the joy we have in the presence of our God because of you? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you again and supply what is lacking in your faith.

For worship. Thank God for the believers who bring you joy. Pray for them to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,

Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus. Key words. A prayer addressed to the Father and the Son together.

Direct our way to you. Key words. “Direct” (kateuthynō, make straight, clear the path). Satan had blocked the way (2:18); God can open it. Remarkably, the verb is singular in Greek, though it has two subjects: God and Father, and our Lord Jesus. The Father and the Son act as one. An early witness to the unity of the Father and the Son, and so to Christ’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are one person. They are distinct persons who act as one God.

In a sentence. Now may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to direct your way today. He can clear any obstacle.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love. Key words. Love grows as the Lord makes it grow. “Increase” (pleonazō) and “abound” (perisseuō, overflow). A flood of love.

For one another and for all. Key words. Fellow believers first, and also all people, including persecutors.

As we do for you. Key words. Paul’s love is the model.

So that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness. Key words. Love leads to holiness. “Establish” (stērizō, strengthen). Blameless: without just accusation.

Before our God and Father. Key words. In his presence, at the judgement.

At the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints. Key words. Christ’s return (parousia). His saints (holy ones): either angels, who accompany him (Matthew 25:31; Zechariah 14:5), or believers who have died, whom he brings with him (4:14), or both.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). Verdict: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blamelessness is achieved by us alone. The Lord establishes it.

In a sentence. May the Lord make your love increase and overflow for each other and for everyone else, just as ours does for you. May he strengthen your hearts so that you will be blameless and holy in the presence of our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

For worship. Pray this prayer for your church: overflowing love, and hearts established in holiness for Christ’s coming.

parallels.desc: the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone,<sup>2</sup>and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,<sup>3</sup>that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.<sup>4</sup>For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know.<sup>5</sup>For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.<sup>6</sup>But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—<sup>7</sup>for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.<sup>8</sup>For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God,<sup>10</sup>as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?<sup>11</sup>Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,<sup>12</sup>and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you,<sup>13</sup>so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

4.title: Holy Living and the Blessed Hope
4.overview:
Paul now fills in what he could not teach in a few weeks. First, holiness: God’s will is that they be sanctified, above all by abstaining from sexual immorality, in a city where sex outside marriage was socially normal for men. Sexual sin wrongs a brother or sister, the Lord avenges it, and to reject this teaching is to reject God, who gives his Holy Spirit. Second, love and work: they are already “taught by God” to love one another, and should do so more and more, living quietly, minding their own business and working with their hands, perhaps because some had stopped working while waiting for Christ.

Third, the question that had shaken them: what happens to believers who die before Jesus returns? They are not lost. Christians grieve, but not without hope. Because Jesus died and rose, God will bring the dead with him. At his loud and public coming, the dead in Christ will rise first; then the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord, as citizens go out to welcome a king, and so we will always be with the Lord. Comfort one another with these words.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–8 – The Will of God Is Your Sanctification
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Turning to how they live, Paul asks them to keep growing in the conduct he taught them, the kind of life that delights God. God’s purpose for them is that they become holy, and in particular that they keep clear of sexual immorality, each one learning to govern his own body honourably rather than being driven by desire like people who do not know God, and never exploiting a fellow believer in this area. God takes such wrongs seriously. His call is to holiness, so to dismiss this teaching is to dismiss God himself, who gives them his Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body, and Who Lives In It

Paul grounds Christian sexual ethics not in his own authority or in respectability but in the Holy Spirit, whom God goes on giving into the believer (v.8). The claim on the Christian's body is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in (cf. 1 Cor 6:19-20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property; Paul brought a different account of what a person is, and applied one standard to men and women alike.

Now: Verse 6 names the victim: sexual sin is always something done to a person, and the Lord is an avenger for those who never had redress.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 4 begins to supply what was lacking in their faith (3:10). First, holiness: God’s will is their sanctification, especially sexual purity. Each must control his body in holiness and honour, not in lust like pagans who do not know God, and must not wrong a brother; God calls to holiness and gives his Holy Spirit (vv. 1–8). Second, love and work: they already love one another, but should do so more; and they should live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands, earning the respect of outsiders (vv. 9–12). Third, hope: some of their number had died, and they feared these would miss out when Christ returned. Paul comforts them. Christians grieve, but not without hope, because Jesus died and rose, and God will bring with him those who have died. When the Lord descends with a shout, the trumpet and the archangel’s voice, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air, and so be with the Lord forever. Encourage one another with these words (vv. 13–18).

Finally, then, brothers. Key words. “Finally” (loipon): for the rest, moving to practical teaching. Not the very end.

We ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus. Key words. Gentle (ask) and firm (urge), with the Lord’s authority.

That as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God. Key words. Paul had taught them how to live. The aim: to please God. Christian ethics is not a list of rules but a life that delights God.

Just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. Key words. Praise first, then encouragement to grow. There is always room to grow.

For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus. Key words. “Instructions” (parangeliai, commands, military orders). By Christ’s authority.

What it does not mean. It does not mean pleasing God earns salvation. It is how the saved live.

In a sentence. As for other matters, brothers and sisters, we instructed you how to live in order to please God, as in fact you are living. Now we ask you and urge you in the Lord Jesus to do this more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what would please God most in my day today? Do it more and more.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;

For this is the will of God, your sanctification. Key words. People often wonder about God’s will. Here it is plainly stated: your sanctification (hagiasmos, being made holy). God’s will is less about which job or house, and more about what kind of person you become.

That you abstain from sexual immorality. Key words. “Abstain” (apechomai, keep away from). Sexual immorality (porneia): any sexual activity outside marriage. In the Greek world, sex outside marriage was widely accepted for men. The gospel brought a radically new standard.

That each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor. Key words. To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself,” as the ESV notes. The Greek word (skeuos) means vessel, used of the body (2 Corinthians 4:7) or of a wife (1 Peter 3:7). Either way: sexual self-control, or honourable marriage, rather than lust.

Not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God. Key words. “Passion of lust” (pathos epithymias, the passion of desire). Those who do not know God follow their desires. Those who know God have a reason and power to be pure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sex itself is unholy. Within marriage it is God’s good gift (1 Corinthians 7:3–5; Hebrews 13:4). It means sexual desire must be governed by holiness.

In a sentence. It is God’s will that you should be sanctified: that you should avoid sexual immorality; that each of you should learn to control your own body in a way that is holy and honourable, not in passionate lust like the pagans, who do not know God;

For worship. God’s will for you is holiness. Ask him for purity in thought and action, and for strength against lust.
verseByVerse.note: To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself”; the phrase can be read either way.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.

That no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter. Key words. “Transgress” (hyperbainō, overstep boundaries). “Wrong” (pleonekteō, take advantage of, defraud). Sexual sin is not private. Adultery defrauds a spouse; sex before marriage defrauds a future spouse and the other person. It violates another’s rights.

Because the Lord is an avenger in all these things. Key words. “Avenger” (ekdikos, one who brings justice). God will judge sexual sin (Hebrews 13:4; Ephesians 5:5–6). Even when no human court acts, God sees.

As we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you. Key words. Paul had already taught them this. Sexual ethics was part of basic Christian instruction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sexual sin cannot be forgiven. It can (1 Corinthians 6:11). It means it is serious.

In a sentence. and that in this matter no one should wrong or take advantage of a brother or sister. The Lord will punish all those who commit such sins, as we told you and warned you before.

On a Tuesday. Think of sexual purity as love for others: refusing to take what is not yours.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.

For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Key words. God’s call into salvation is a call to holiness (1 Peter 1:15–16). Impurity (akatharsia, uncleanness) is the opposite of what God called us to.

Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God. Key words. “Disregards” (atheteō, rejects, sets aside). To reject this teaching is not to reject Paul’s opinion, but God’s command.

Who gives his Holy Spirit to you. Key words. Present tense: God keeps giving his Spirit. The Holy Spirit dwells in believers (1 Corinthians 6:19). Sexual sin grieves him. And he gives the power to be holy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sexual sin rejects God. All sin does. But sexual sin is singled out here.

In a sentence. For God did not call us to be impure, but to live a holy life. Therefore, anyone who rejects this instruction does not reject a human being but God, the very God who gives you his Holy Spirit.

For worship. Thank God for the gift of his Holy Spirit. Ask him for power to live holy today.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:9–12 – Brotherly Love and the Quiet Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They need no teaching about loving one another, because God has taught them and they already love believers throughout Macedonia; Paul urges them to do so more and more. They should also aim to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Covenant, Landed

Theodidaktoi appears nowhere in Greek literature before this letter; Paul seems to have coined it. He is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah's new covenant promise — I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts, and they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest (Jer 31:33-34).

That is a considerable claim to make about a congregation of ex-pagans a few months old. Paul says the promised covenant has visibly arrived among them — and his evidence is not their doctrine but their love, which is the more striking because he was driven out before he could teach them much. What they know, God taught them from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Why would a church need telling to work? Almost certainly because of the subject of the next paragraph. If the Lord is returning imminently, why keep a trade, why plan, why save? The problem worsened rather than resolved: in the second letter Paul has to deal with people who are 'not busy at work, but busybodies', and rules that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thess 3:10-12). And 'work with your hands' was an affront to Greek sensibility — manual labour was for slaves and the poor, not for men with philosophical pretensions.

Now: The principle is one the letter keeps insisting on: expecting the Lord's return should make a Christian more reliable, not less. Idleness is treated here as a failure of love, because the idle man's food comes from somewhere and the somewhere is his brothers. Note too the ambition Paul actually commends — philotimeisthai hesychazein, make it your point of honour to be unremarkable. The New Testament's aim for most Christians is not a platform but ordinary competence: your own work done well, your own business minded, and nobody made poorer for having you around.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,

Now concerning brotherly love. Key words. “Brotherly love” (philadelphia): love for fellow believers as family. Perhaps they had asked about it.

You have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Key words. “Taught by God” (theodidaktos): a word perhaps coined by Paul. God himself taught them love, through the gospel and the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33–34; John 6:45; 1 John 2:27). The new covenant promise fulfilled.

For that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. Key words. Their love reached beyond their own church, perhaps through hospitality to travellers and financial help.

But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more. Key words. Love can always grow.

What it does not mean. It does not mean teaching about love is unnecessary. It means God’s inner teaching makes love natural to believers.

In a sentence. Now about your love for one another we do not need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love each other. And in fact, you do love all of God’s family throughout Macedonia. Yet we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more,

On a Tuesday. Show brotherly love today to a believer from another church.

verseByVerse.quote: and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.

And to aspire to live quietly. Key words. A paradox: be ambitious (philotimeomai) to be quiet (hēsychazō). Make it your ambition not to be a busybody or agitator.

And to mind your own affairs. Key words. Do not meddle in others’ business (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

And to work with your hands, as we instructed you. Key words. Some Thessalonians seem to have stopped working, perhaps because they thought Christ was returning immediately, or because they expected wealthier believers to support them (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). Greeks often despised manual work; Paul honours it.

So that you may walk properly before outsiders. Key words. “Properly” (euschēmonōs, decently, respectably). Idle believers bring the gospel into disrepute.

And be dependent on no one. Key words. Self-supporting, so as not to burden others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never receive help. Those who cannot work should be supported. It means those who can work should.

In a sentence. and to make it your ambition to lead a quiet life: you should mind your own business and work with your hands, just as we told you, so that your daily life may win the respect of outsiders and so that you will not be dependent on anybody.

For worship. Thank God for the gift of work. Do your work today as service to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some believers in Thessalonica had died, and the church feared they would miss the Lord’s return. Paul writes so that they will not mourn like people with no hope. Because Jesus died and rose, God will bring the believers who have died with him. On the Lord’s authority Paul assures them that the living will have no advantage over the dead. The Lord will descend from heaven with a shout of command, the archangel’s voice and God’s trumpet; the dead in Christ will rise first, then the living will be gathered up together with them to meet the Lord, and from then on they will always be with him. They are to use this truth to comfort one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Meeting on the Road

‘To meet the Lord’ (v.17) is the language of a city's delegation going out along the road to greet an arriving king and escort him in (cf. Acts 28:15). The passage gives one loud, public, personal arrival at which the Christian dead are raised first; it gives no timetable, and it settles less of the wider debate about the order of the last things than is often claimed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Against the bleak tomb inscriptions of that world, a Christian funeral in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else altogether.

Now: Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope (v.13); and the passage is for comforting one another at gravesides (v.18), not for building charts.

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.

But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers. Key words. A new topic, probably raised by Timothy’s report.

About those who are asleep. Key words. “Asleep” was a common Christian way of speaking of believers who had died, pointing to their waking at the resurrection (John 11:11; Acts 7:60; 1 Corinthians 15:18). Some Thessalonian believers had died since Paul left, perhaps through persecution.

That you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. Key words. “Grieve” (lypeō). Paul does not forbid grief; he forbids hopeless grief. Pagan grave inscriptions often expressed despair: one reads, “I was not, I became, I am not, I care not.” Christians grieve, but with hope.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some take “asleep” to mean the souls of the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Verdict: Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The souls of believers are immediately with Christ, consciously and joyfully (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). God will bring them with Jesus (v. 14): they are with him now. Their bodies sleep until the resurrection (Westminster 32.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not mourn. Jesus wept (John 11:35). Grief is love’s response to loss.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope.

On a Tuesday. If you grieve a believer who has died, grieve with hope. They are with Christ, and you will see them again.
verseByVerse.note: “Asleep” was a common Christian way of speaking of believers who had died.

verseByVerse.quote: For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again. Key words. The foundation of hope. Notice Paul says Jesus died, not fell asleep. Jesus experienced death in all its horror, so that for believers it might become sleep.

Even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. Key words. Because he rose, they will rise. God will bring them with Jesus at his return: their souls, now with him, will accompany him, to be reunited with their raised bodies. “Through Jesus”: through his saving work, or those who fell asleep through Jesus, as believers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers who die miss Christ’s return. They will be with him when he comes.

In a sentence. For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him.

For worship. Thank God that because Jesus rose, those who died in him will rise too.

verseByVerse.quote: For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.

For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord. Key words. Either a saying of Jesus not recorded in the Gospels, or a revelation to Paul, or a summary of Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 24:30–31). Either way, with the Lord’s authority.

That we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord. Key words. Paul includes himself, not because he knew he would be alive, but as one of those who might be. Every generation lives ready.

Will not precede those who have fallen asleep. Key words. “Precede” (phthanō, get ahead of). The living will have no advantage over the dead.

For the Lord himself will descend from heaven. Key words. The Lord himself: personally, not a messenger. From heaven, where he now reigns (1:10; Acts 1:11).

With a cry of command. Key words. “Cry of command” (keleusma, a shout of command, as a general to troops, or a captain to rowers). Perhaps the voice that raises the dead (John 5:28–29).

With the voice of an archangel. Key words. A chief angel, perhaps Michael (Jude 9).

And with the sound of the trumpet of God. Key words. The last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52; Matthew 24:31). Trumpets summoned God’s people and announced God’s coming (Exodus 19:16).

And the dead in Christ will rise first. Key words. First, before the living are caught up. The bodies of believers who died are raised.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers will not be raised. All will be raised (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15). Paul speaks here of believers only.

In a sentence. According to the Lord’s word, we tell you that we who are still alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first.

For worship. Imagine the shout, the archangel, the trumpet. The Lord himself is coming. Worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.

Then we who are alive, who are left. Key words. After the dead are raised.

Will be caught up together with them in the clouds. Key words. “Caught up” (harpazō, snatched up, seized). The Latin translation is rapiemur, from which the word rapture. Together with them: living and raised believers reunited. In the clouds: often the sign of God’s presence (Exodus 19:9; Acts 1:9; Daniel 7:13).

To meet the Lord in the air. Key words. “Meet” (apantēsis) was the word used of citizens going out to welcome an arriving emperor or dignitary and escort him back into the city (as in Matthew 25:6 and Acts 28:15). Believers rise to welcome Christ and accompany him as he comes to earth in triumph, not to be taken away elsewhere.

And so we will always be with the Lord. Key words. The heart of the hope: forever with Christ. Not mainly a place, but a person.

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists teach a secret, pre-tribulation rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers to heaven, leaving the world to a seven-year tribulation, before returning visibly with them. Verdict: This passage describes the loudest, most public event imaginable: a shout, an archangel’s voice, God’s trumpet. Nothing is secret. The word “meet” describes going out to welcome a coming king and escort him back, which points to Christ’s coming to earth, not to a removal to heaven. The same events (trumpet, gathering of the elect, coming on the clouds) describe Christ’s one visible return in Matthew 24:30–31. Scripture teaches one return of Christ, at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, the living changed and caught up, and all are judged (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The rapture is real, but it is part of that one glorious coming, not a separate secret event.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know the date. It will come like a thief (5:2).

In a sentence. After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord for ever.

On a Tuesday. You will always be with the Lord. Let that hope steady you today.
verseByVerse.note: “Meet” was the word used of citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him into the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another with these words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore encourage one another with these words.

Therefore encourage one another with these words. Key words. “Encourage” (parakaleō, comfort, exhort). The purpose of teaching on the second coming is not speculation or charts, but comfort. Christians should comfort the grieving with the truth of Christ’s return and the resurrection. Paul expected these words to be used at funerals and in sorrow.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prophecy is only for comfort. It also calls to readiness (5:6). But comfort is the main application here.

In a sentence. Therefore encourage one another with these words.

For worship. Share these verses with someone who is grieving a believer’s death. Comfort them with the hope of Christ’s return.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more.<sup>2</sup>For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.<sup>3</sup>For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality;<sup>4</sup>that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor,<sup>5</sup>not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;<sup>6</sup>that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.<sup>7</sup>For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness.<sup>8</sup>Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.<sup>9</sup>Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another,<sup>10</sup>for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,<sup>11</sup>and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you,<sup>12</sup>so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.<sup>13</sup>But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.<sup>14</sup>For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.<sup>15</sup>For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep.<sup>16</sup>For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.<sup>17</sup>Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.<sup>18</sup>Therefore encourage one another with these words.

5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview:
After answering what happens to believers who die, Paul answers the next question, “When?”, by declining to give a date. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, suddenly, on a world saying “peace and security”. But believers are children of the day, so it will not catch them unprepared. They are to stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope, because God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through Jesus, who died for them.

Then a run of instructions for church life: respect those who lead and work hard among you; warn the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all; never repay evil; rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in everything; do not quench the Spirit, but test everything and keep what is good. The letter ends with a prayer that the God of peace will make them wholly holy, and a promise: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They know that the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a thief in the night, and that sudden ruin will fall on those who feel secure. But believers are not in darkness, to be taken by surprise; they belong to the day. So they must stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God has not appointed them to wrath but to salvation through Christ, who died for them so that, whether alive or dead at his coming, they will live with him. So they should encourage and build up one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Destined for Wrath

God's purpose for his people was settled in advance, and settled on salvation rather than wrath (v.9) — not because of their performance but because the Lord Jesus ‘died for us’ (v.10), the only place in the letter where Paul states the substitution directly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Peace and security’ was close to an imperial slogan, and Paul names it as the moment of collapse.

Now: Paul tells them what they are — children of the day — before he tells them to stay awake (vv.5–6). Getting that order backwards is what produces exhausted Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 5 turns from comfort about the dead to readiness for the living. First, the timing: no one knows when the day of the Lord will come; it will come like a thief, suddenly, when people feel secure, bringing destruction they cannot escape (vv. 1–3). But believers are children of light, not darkness; so they must stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope. God has not appointed them to wrath but to salvation through Christ, who died for them so that, alive or dead, they will live with him. So encourage one another (vv. 4–11). Second, life in the church: respect your leaders, live at peace, warn the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient, never repay evil, rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances, do not quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and keep away from evil (vv. 12–22). Finally, a prayer that the God of peace will sanctify them completely and keep them blameless for Christ’s coming, with the assurance that he who calls them is faithful and will do it (vv. 23–28).

Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers. Key words. “Times” (chronoi, periods of time) and “seasons” (kairoi, appointed moments). When will it happen? Jesus said the same words: it is not for you to know the times or seasons (Acts 1:7).

You have no need to have anything written to you. Key words. They already knew the essential point.

For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. Key words. The day of the Lord: the Old Testament phrase for God’s great day of judgement and salvation (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31; Zephaniah 1:14), now identified with Christ’s return. Like a thief: unexpected, unannounced (Matthew 24:43; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 16:15). No one can predict the date.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the day will be secret. It will be sudden, but visible to all.

In a sentence. Now, brothers and sisters, about times and dates we do not need to write to you, for you know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

On a Tuesday. Do not try to calculate the date of Christ’s return. Be ready for it today.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While people are saying, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

While people are saying, “There is peace and security.” Key words. “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order: the Pax Romana and the security Rome promised its subjects. People feel safe, as in the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37–39). False prophets in Jeremiah’s day cried peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).

Then sudden destruction will come upon them. Key words. “Destruction” (olethros, ruin): not annihilation, but eternal loss (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

As labor pains come upon a pregnant woman. Key words. Labour pains come suddenly, and once begun, cannot be stopped. And they come to a woman who knows they are coming, but not exactly when.

And they will not escape. Key words. Emphatic in Greek: they will by no means escape.

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace is bad. It means false security apart from God is deadly.

In a sentence. While people are saying, “Peace and safety,” destruction will come on them suddenly, as labour pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

For worship. Pray for people around you who feel secure without God. Ask God to wake them before it is too late.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order.

parallels.desc: Peace, peace, when there is no peace

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.

But you are not in darkness, brothers. Key words. Darkness: ignorance, sin, unbelief.

For that day to surprise you like a thief. Key words. Believers do not know the date, but they will not be caught unprepared. A thief surprises only those who are asleep.

For you are all children of light, children of the day. Key words. A Hebrew idiom: sons of light means belonging to light, characterised by it (Ephesians 5:8; John 12:36). Believers belong to the coming day of Christ. All: every believer.

We are not of the night or of the darkness. Key words. Paul includes himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are already perfect. It means they belong to a different realm.

In a sentence. But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness so that this day should surprise you like a thief. You are all children of the light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to the darkness.

On a Tuesday. You are a child of the light. Live in the light today, with nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.

So then let us not sleep, as others do. Key words. Sleep here is spiritual carelessness, not death as in chapter 4. Unbelievers are spiritually asleep.

But let us keep awake and be sober. Key words. “Keep awake” (grēgoreō, watch, be alert). “Be sober” (nēphō, clear-headed, self-controlled). Jesus’ repeated command (Mark 13:33–37).

For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night. Key words. Night is when people sleep and get drunk. Believers belong to the day, and should behave accordingly (Romans 13:12–13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never sleep or relax. It means they should never be spiritually careless.

In a sentence. So then, let us not be like others, who are asleep, but let us be awake and sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night.

For worship. Ask God to keep you spiritually awake and clear-headed today.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.

But since we belong to the day, let us be sober. Key words. Identity leads to conduct.

Having put on the breastplate of faith and love. Key words. A soldier on night watch wears armour. The breastplate protects the heart: faith in God and love for others.

And for a helmet the hope of salvation. Key words. The helmet protects the head: the sure hope of final salvation guards the mind from despair and doubt (Isaiah 59:17; Ephesians 6:14–17). Faith, love and hope again (1:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean hope is uncertain wishing. It is confident expectation.

In a sentence. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on faith and love as a breastplate, and the hope of salvation as a helmet.

On a Tuesday. Put on your armour today: faith in God, love for others, hope of salvation.

parallels.desc: righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.

For God has not destined us for wrath. Key words. “Destined” (tithēmi, appointed). Wrath: God’s final judgement (1:10). God did not appoint believers to it.

But to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. God appointed them to salvation: election again (1:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:13).

Who died for us. Key words. “For us” (hyper hēmōn, in our place). The basis of salvation: Christ’s substitutionary death.

So that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him. Key words. Awake or asleep: alive or dead at Christ’s return (connecting to 4:13–18). Either way, we will live with him. No believer misses out.

Where Christians differ: not destined for wrath. Some use this verse to argue that believers will be raptured before a future tribulation. Verdict: The wrath here is God’s final judgement on the ungodly, from which Christ’s death saves believers (1:10; Romans 5:9). It does not promise exemption from suffering or persecution before the end; the Thessalonians were already suffering (3:3). Believers will be delivered from God’s wrath, not from all tribulation (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers can live carelessly. Those destined for salvation live as children of the day.

In a sentence. For God did not appoint us to suffer wrath but to receive salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

For worship. Thank God that he destined you for salvation, not wrath, because Christ died for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.

Therefore encourage one another. Key words. The same command as 4:18. The second coming is a source of encouragement.

And build one another up. Key words. “Build up” (oikodomeō). Every believer is a builder of others.

Just as you are doing. Key words. Praise and encouragement to continue.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only leaders encourage. All believers do.

In a sentence. Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.

On a Tuesday. Encourage one fellow believer today with the hope of Christ’s return.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to respect and love those who labour among them, lead them and admonish them, and to live at peace. They should warn the idle, encourage the timid, help the weak and be patient with everyone; never repay evil for evil but always seek good. They are to rejoice always, pray continually and give thanks in every circumstance, which is God’s will in Christ. They must not quench the Spirit or despise prophecy, but test everything, holding on to what is good and avoiding every kind of evil.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment Instead of Either Extreme

Verses 19–22 refuse both easy positions: not contempt for what the Spirit gives, and not credulity, but testing — holding fast what is good and abstaining from what is bad. A church asked to be both open and awake has the harder, better task.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation only months old already had people labouring, leading and admonishing, honoured ‘because of their work’ (v.13).

Now: Verse 14 asks every member, not only leaders, to read the person in front of them: the idle need admonishing, the fainthearted encouraging, the weak holding up. And verse 18 asks for thanks in all circumstances, not for them.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.

We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you. Key words. Church leaders, probably elders, though the word is not used. Three descriptions: they labour (kopiaō, work hard), are over you in the Lord (proistēmi, lead, care for), and admonish you (noutheteō, warn, instruct). “Respect” (literally know them, recognise them).

And to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Key words. “Very highly” (hyperekperissou, beyond all measure). Not because of their personality, but because of their work. With love, not just duty.

Be at peace among yourselves. Key words. Perhaps some tension between leaders and the idle (v. 14). Peace in the church honours leaders and Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean leaders are above correction. It means they deserve honour and love.

In a sentence. Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to acknowledge those who work hard among you, who care for you in the Lord and who admonish you. Hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work. Live in peace with each other.

For worship. Thank God for your church leaders. Tell one of them this week that you appreciate their work.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.

And we urge you, brothers. Key words. All believers, not just leaders, care for one another.

Admonish the idle. Key words. “Idle” (ataktoi, disorderly, out of line, like soldiers breaking ranks) may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting Christ’s immediate return (4:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). Warn them.

Encourage the fainthearted. Key words. “Fainthearted” (oligopsychoi, small-souled, discouraged, anxious). Perhaps those grieving or afraid. Comfort them.

Help the weak. Key words. “Help” (antechomai, hold on to, support). The spiritually or physically weak.

Be patient with them all. Key words. “Patient” (makrothymeō, long-suffering). Different people need different care: warning for some, comfort for others, support for others, patience for all. Wise pastoral care diagnoses before it treats.

What it does not mean. It does not mean one approach fits all. Warning the fainthearted crushes them; comforting the idle confirms them.

In a sentence. And we urge you, brothers and sisters, warn those who are idle and disruptive, encourage the disheartened, help the weak, be patient with everyone.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know. Do they need warning, encouragement, or help? Give it with patience.
verseByVerse.note: “Idle” may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s imminent return.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.

See that no one repays anyone evil for evil. Key words. The church must watch that no one takes revenge (Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9; Matthew 5:38–44). Persecuted believers would be tempted to retaliate.

But always seek to do good to one another and to everyone. Key words. “Seek” (diōkō, pursue, chase). Actively pursue doing good, to believers and to everyone, including persecutors.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring justice. Governments punish evil (Romans 13:4). It means personal revenge is forbidden.

In a sentence. Make sure that nobody pays back wrong for wrong, but always strive to do what is good for each other and for everyone else.

For worship. Is someone you want to pay back? Ask God for grace to do them good instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

Rejoice always. Key words. The shortest verse in the Greek New Testament (by letters). Always: even in persecution and grief. Possible only because joy is in the Lord (Philippians 4:4).

Pray without ceasing. Key words. “Without ceasing” (adialeiptōs, constantly, like a recurring cough). Not non-stop words, but a life of constant communion with God, turning to him all day long, and regular times of prayer.

Give thanks in all circumstances. Key words. In all circumstances, not for all circumstances: we do not thank God for evil, but in every situation we find reason to thank him, because he is at work (Romans 8:28).

For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you. Key words. Another clear statement of God’s will (4:3). God’s will is joy, prayer and thanksgiving. In Christ Jesus: these are possible through him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faking happiness or denying sorrow. Christians lament too. But beneath lament is joy and thanks.

In a sentence. Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

For worship. Practise all three today: find reasons to rejoice, turn to God often, and give thanks in every situation.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.

Do not quench the Spirit. Key words. “Quench” (sbennymi, put out, as a fire). The Spirit is like fire (Acts 2:3). He can be stifled by sin, neglect, or suppressing his work in the church.

Do not despise prophecies. Key words. Some in Thessalonica may have been dismissing prophetic words, perhaps after abuses or false predictions about Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:2).

But test everything. Key words. “Test” (dokimazō, examine, as metal is tested). Not every claimed word from God is genuine (1 John 4:1). Test it by Scripture and the apostolic gospel.

Hold fast what is good. Key words. Keep what passes the test.

Abstain from every form of evil. Key words. Reject what fails, and evil in every form.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Continuationists see here a command for churches to welcome prophecy today; some cessationists dismiss the passage. Verdict: In the apostolic churches, before the New Testament was complete, prophecy was an active gift, and Paul commanded the church neither to despise nor accept it uncritically. With the completion of Scripture, revelatory prophecy has ceased (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But the principles remain: do not quench the Spirit, who speaks through the word; test every teaching and claim by Scripture; hold to what is good. These apply to preaching, teaching and every claim of spiritual guidance today. This view is held with charity toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being suspicious of everything. It means discernment.

In a sentence. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear today, from preachers, books, podcasts, by Scripture. Keep what is good.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the God of peace will make them holy through and through and keep them whole and blameless until the coming of the Lord Jesus; the God who calls them is faithful and will do it. He asks for their prayers, sends greetings with a holy kiss, insists that the letter be read to all the believers, and ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole Persons, and Who Does the Keeping

‘Spirit and soul and body’ (v.23) is a way of saying the whole of you, and they are to be kept — passive — by the God who calls them and is faithful (v.24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath of verse 27 ensured the letter reached every believer, the illiterate and the fainthearted included.

Now: The holy kiss for all the brothers (v.26) is a quiet demolition of rank: you cannot greet someone as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.

Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely. Key words. The God of peace: who makes peace with sinners and gives peace. Himself: sanctification is ultimately his work. “Completely” (holoteleis, wholly, through and through): every part.

And may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless. Key words. The whole person. “Kept” (tēreō, guarded, preserved). Blameless: without fault.

At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The goal: ready for his return.

He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it. Key words. The guarantee. God does not call and then abandon. What he begins, he completes (Philippians 1:6; 1 Corinthians 1:8–9).

Where Christians differ: spirit, soul and body. Some (trichotomists) take this to mean humans have three distinct parts: spirit, soul and body. Others (dichotomists) hold two: body and soul (or spirit). Verdict: Scripture usually describes humans as body and soul, or body and spirit, using soul and spirit interchangeably (Matthew 10:28; 1 Corinthians 7:34; Ecclesiastes 12:7). Paul here stresses the whole person, every aspect, not giving a technical anatomy. The majority Reformed view is that humans are a unity of body and soul (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 10; Larger Catechism Q. 17).

Where Christians differ: entire sanctification. Some in the Wesleyan tradition take this verse to teach that believers can be sanctified entirely in this life, free from sin. Verdict: Paul prays for complete sanctification, and God will accomplish it, at the coming of Christ. In this life, believers grow in holiness but remain sinners (1 John 1:8). Sanctification is complete at glorification (Philippians 3:12; Westminster 13.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. But it rests our hope on God’s faithfulness, not our strength.

In a sentence. May God himself, the God of peace, sanctify you through and through. May your whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

For worship. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it. Rest in that promise today.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.

Brothers, pray for us. Key words. Paul, who has prayed for them, now asks their prayers. Mutual intercession.

Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. Key words. The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church (Romans 16:16). All: including the idle and the fainthearted.

I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. Key words. A solemn charge. Perhaps some leaders might not share it with everyone, or some members could not read. Letters were read aloud in church gatherings. Paul’s letter was to be treated as authoritative, like Scripture read in the synagogue (Colossians 4:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture is only for leaders. It is for all God’s people.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, pray for us. Greet all God’s people with a holy kiss. Paul charges you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor and for missionaries today. And make sure Scripture is read in your home.
verseByVerse.note: The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Key words. The letter began with grace (1:1) and ends with it. Everything in between, comfort, warning, instruction, flows from grace. The final word for the church is not a command, but a gift.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace is earned by the obedience commanded in the letter. Grace makes that obedience possible.

In a sentence. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

For worship. Receive this blessing today: the grace of the Lord Jesus is with you.
